newsitem.title: USA: N.J. primary to chose Whitman opponent.
newsitem.headline: N.J. primary to chose Whitman opponent.

text.p: New Jersey voters Tuesday will select one of three Democrats vying for the chance to challenge popular Republican incumbent Gov. Christine Whitman in a November general election.

Whitman, whose ouster of Democrat Jim Florio in 1993 on the strength of a promised tax cut vaulted her to national prominence, is heavily favoured to win re-election. But her would-be challengers are hoping to exploit what they see as her vulnerabilities stemming from the income tax cut, including higher local property tax rates and controversial state finance decisions.

Whitman remains the "strong favourite," Rider University political scientist David Rebovich said. However, he said, "The race will probably be closer than any of us would have contemplated a year ago."

Major Democratic candidates vying to challenge Whitman are Representative Robert Andrews; James McGreevey, a state senator and mayor of Woodbridge; and former Morris County prosecutor Michael Murphy. According to a Mason-Dixon poll for News 12 New Jersey television released last week, Andrews led among likely Democratic voters with 27 percent support.

McGreevey was second with 22, followed by Murphy with 16. But a large undecided block -- 35 percent -- and McGreevey's edge in support among party loyalists able to turn out the vote left the outcome far from certain.

Andrews, defending a strong fiscally conservative stance, and McGreevey, courting traditional Democratic voters, spent much of the spring battling for the support of politically powerful county Democratic organisations.
McGreevey emerged with the edge in endorsements. But the insiders battle left an opportunity for Murphy to build unexpected momentum as a candidate unbeholden to the Democratic party bosses.

"I don't have to deal with them before I take a position," Murphy said at a campaign event Friday in Cherry Hill. He has scored a public relations coup with television ads portraying Andrews and McGreevey as squabbling children and won the endorsement of some important newspapers circulating in the state, including the Philadelphia Inquirer.

Murphy's surge may end up hurting McGreevey most by cutting into his base of supporters in northern New Jersey, Rebovich said. Andrews, a resident of the Philadelphia suburb of Haddon Heights, New Jersey, is strongest in the less populous southern half of the state.

Whitman has consistently sought to remind voters she has delivered on her promise of a 30 percent cut in state income taxes, but she has been attacked for rises in local property taxes to make up for state spending cuts, privatisation of state activities and a controversial plan to finance state pension obligations through a bond sale.

Andrews pledged early in the campaign not to raise taxes, while McGreevey has campaigned on a plan to increase education spending and Murphy is proposing a 25-cent-per-pack tax on cigarettes to finance more spending on schools.
New Jersey's stubbornly high auto insurance rates also remain a sore point among voters.
"If the field hasn't yielded a crop, it's time to change the farmer," McGreevey said in a Trenton church Sunday.
Despite the attacks, the News 12 New Jersey poll showed Whitman easily outdistancing any of her three likely opponents in the fall election.
